title: The sunshine vitamin
text: Vitamin D is unusual among nutrients: the main source is not the plate but the {{1}}. Ultraviolet light in the skin converts a cholesterol-like molecule into the vitamin, which the body then {{2}} into the hormone that manages calcium — bones first, but also muscles and immune cells. Geography {{3}}. Darker skin protects against strong sun and therefore makes vitamin D more slowly; populations that migrated to grey latitudes evolved paler skin precisely to {{4}} production, and anyone living north of roughly Madrid or Beijing makes essentially nothing from October to March. The {{5}} is modern life: office work, sunscreen and indoor living have made deficiency {{6}} even in sunny countries, and winter supplements are now routine advice in Britain. The dose debates {{7}}: agencies disagree about targets, and enthusiastic claims about vitamin D curing everything from depression to cancer have generally {{8}} under trial. What survives is solid enough: keep it adequate for bones and muscles, take a little in winter, and remember that the best supplement ever designed rises every morning and costs nothing.

gaps.explanation: 'not the plate but the sky' — the sun overhead; the sentence contrasts food with sunlight.
'the body then processes it into the hormone' — converts it through its systems; profess = claim.
'Geography counts' — matters, makes a difference; amount takes 'to', recount = tell again.
'paler skin to maximise production' — get the most from weak sun; minimise is the exact opposite.
'the complication is modern life' — the factor that makes it harder; complexion = skin colouring.
'made deficiency common' — widespread; the adjective follows 'made…'; commonly is the adverb and communal means shared.
'the dose debates continue' — are still running; contend = argue, and debates do not 'contend' themselves.
'claims have evaporated under trial' — melted away when tested; excavate = dig up.
